Explain why a voltmeter goes in parallel and an ammeter goes in series. Include the danger of placing an ammeter across a supply.
questions.modelAnswer: Voltage is a potential difference between two points, so the voltmeter is placed across them and has high input resistance to draw little current. An ammeter measures current through a path and has low internal resistance, so it is inserted in series. Across a supply it can create a near-short, blow a fuse, damage equipment or cause injury.
rubric: Explains voltage measurement between two points.
Explains current measurement through a path.
Mentions high voltmeter and low ammeter internal resistance.
questions.hint: Compare high and low meter resistance.
questions.hint2: Voltage: parallel. Current: series. Ammeter across supply: near-short.

questions.question: A 5 V Arduino circuit uses a 2 V LED at 10 mA. Calculate the series resistor and explain why the resistor and pin rating matter.
questions.modelAnswer: The resistor drops 5 − 2 = 3 V. Convert 10 mA to 0.010 A, then R = 3/0.010 = 300 Ω ideal. The resistor limits LED and pin current. Choose an available value that respects component ratings and check resistor dissipation and the Uno's recommended pin current.
questions.source: Resistors slides 17–18; CSP19 reviewer pages 7–8 and 13

questions.question: Compare series and parallel resistor networks: current, voltage, equivalent resistance and what happens when one path opens.
questions.modelAnswer: Series components share one path and the same current; voltage drops add to the source voltage, resistances add, and one open stops the path. Parallel components share two nodes and the same voltage; currents divide and branch currents add, equivalent resistance is below the smallest branch resistance, and another branch can remain active when one opens.
rubric: States the current rule for each network.
States the voltage rule for each network.
Explains the effect of an open path.
questions.hint2: Series: same current, add R. Parallel: same voltage, lower equivalent R.

questions.question: Describe a systematic first pass when an Arduino breadboard circuit fails to work.
questions.modelAnswer: Identify supply, ground, component orientation and nodes in the schematic. Measure supply voltage in the correct meter mode. Verify breadboard groups and split rails; check LED, diode and electrolytic polarity. Recalculate resistor values and unit conversions. Confirm pin choice, sketch logic and shared ground. Power down before moving wires; change and retest one thing at a time.
rubric: Checks breadboard connectivity and component polarity.
Checks values, units, pin and sketch.
Powers down before rewiring and changes one thing at a time.
questions.hint2: Measure supply; verify rails and polarity; recalculate; check pins; retest one change.
